newsitem.title: USA: Okla. HFA hopes document will help deal close soon.
newsitem.headline: Okla. HFA hopes document will help deal close soon.

text.p: Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency officials are confident that a 1982 document discovered Wednesday morning will clear up concerns that are likely to delay next Tuesday's scheduled closing of a $20 million low-income housing deal.

Neta Stephenson, the housing agency's executive director, said a Tulsa attorney working on an unrelated housing bond deal alerted her agency to discrepancies in figures used to determine target areas, or places most in need of low-income loans.
In non-target areas, only first-time home buyers can qualify for such loans. Oklahoma HFA's figures differed from a 1994 Revenue Proclamation put out by the Internal Revenue Service, she said.

Concerned that the discrepancies may have a negative impact on the offering that priced October 25, Stephenson said the Oklahoma HFA decided to contact U.S. Treasury officials and the IRS before proceeding with the closing.

"Until we knew for sure that everything was okay, it seemed like the best thing to do because we owed that to our bond holders," Stephenson said. "The IRS and the Treasury were extremely good to work with."
Following Tuesday's meeting, Oklahoma housing officials on Wednesday discovered a October 1982 report by Nancy Anthony Ph.D.

The housing agency had commmissioned the report on the data requirements necessary for proposed target areas for the 1982 Single Family Bond Program, according to Jack Lawrence, outside general counsel to Oklahoma HFA. The document was submitted to the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the IRS. The report was approved in December 1982, Lawrence said.

"It had been approved by the Federal government back at that time and it is our understanding that it remains in effect until rescinded," Lawrence said, adding that the document has not been rescinded. The figures in the 1982 study differ in only minor ways from figures the agency used in association with its bond issue, he said.

Stephenson said IRS regulations allow states to conduct their own, more indepth studies to determine "chronic economic distress areas." Oklahoma HFA plans to bring the document to the attention of Treasury and IRS officials soon, she said.
Though Lawrence and Stephenson are hopeful that the deal will close soon, they said it is unlikely that it will close Tuesday as scheduled.
